screens.title: Working with Data Types and Conversions
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll build a clear mental model of how VEX represents data and how Houdini moves values between types and attribute classes. We'll review the basic VEX types — integer, float, vectors of two, three and four components, and strings — and then focus on how conversions happen, both implicitly and when you explicitly cast. You will see practical examples of where implicit casting helps and where it silently causes data loss, and we'll establish safe patterns you can use right away. We'll also cover attribute scope: point, primitive, vertex and detail, and how functions like prim, point, and detail enable reading across those scopes. Finally, we'll walk through controlled attribute writes using setpointattrib and related functions, so you can create or modify attributes on other components without surprises. By the end you will be able to choose the correct type, avoid common mismatches, and explain why explicit casts sometimes prevent subtle bugs. Consider a simple float driving color: small choices here change whether color becomes a uniform grey or an intended RGB value. Keep that contrast in mind as you explore the examples.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives frame practical skills you can apply immediately when authoring VEX. First, you will accurately identify and use VEX native types: integers, floats, vector2, vector, vector4 and strings. This means you will choose the correct storage type for positions, UVs, colors, and identifiers to avoid downstream errors. Second, you'll explain and demonstrate both implicit and explicit conversions. You will show examples that reveal safe broadcasting and places where implicit truncation hides precision loss. Third, you'll understand attribute scope and class — point, primitive, vertex and detail — and how attribute class affects where data lives and how functions access it. You will practice reading a primitive attribute while running over points and vice versa. Fourth, you'll use the explicit set*attrib functions safely: setpointattrib, setprimattrib, setvertexattrib and setdetailattrib, knowing when these are necessary and what their cost is compared to direct assignments. Each objective ties a conceptual idea to an actionable outcome so you can verify competency in the Geometry Spreadsheet and in a wrangle node.

screens.title: VEX data types: scalar and vector families
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the primary VEX types and place them into practical contexts you’ll use every day. An int is a whole number used for counts, indices, or discrete flags. A float stores real numbers with fractional precision and is the workhorse for measurements and continuous values. Vector2 stores two floats, useful for UV coordinates; vector stores three floats and is the canonical type for positions, normals and 3D directions; vector4 packs four floats and commonly represents color with alpha. String is used for text, like material names or identifiers. Each type has semantic meaning: choose int for loop counters and array indexes, float for scale factors and weights, vector for spatial data and color triples, and string for names. A common mistake is using a vector where a float was intended, which complicates math operations and causes type errors. Another pitfall is storing an index as a float – it may work in some contexts but can create subtle bugs when compared or used as an index. To ground this, consider @P as a vector holding vertex positions, @uv as a vector2 for texture coordinates, and @Cd as a vector for color. When you pick types with intention, your wrangles become clearer and less error-prone. Try to name attributes in a way that hints at their type, such as prim_id_float or global_scale_int, so the spreadsheet tells the story.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › VEX data types
Definition
Scalar vs Vector families
Clear definitions reduce type errors and improve readability.
int
Whole numbers for counts, indices, and discrete states.
float
Real numbers with fractional precision for weights and measures.
vector2 / vector / vector4
Multi-component containers for UVs, positions/normals, and RGBA colors respectively.
string
Textual identifiers like material names or tags.
Common mistake

Using a vector when a scalar was intended makes math and comparisons harder and may produce type errors in functions that expect scalars.

Concrete examples
Positions
@P is a vector representing XYZ coordinates of a point.
Texture coords
@uv is a vector2 for U and V texture coordinates.
Color
@Cd is a vector; @Cd.w or vector4 holds alpha when needed.
Identifiers
Use strings for names and material labels accessed with prim() or detail().
Key Takeaway

Name attributes with type hints and pick types that reflect the underlying meaning — it saves time and prevents errors.

screens.title: Implicit conversions — convenience and risk
screens.narratorSegment: Implicit conversions are a convenience built into VEX, but they carry trade-offs you must understand. When you assign a float to an int, VEX truncates the fractional part. When you assign a float to a vector, the float broadcasts to every component producing a uniform vector. These behaviors are handy: you can set a uniform color or a uniform offset with a single scalar. But implicit truncation can hide logic errors. For example, assigning 5.7 to an int yields 5, which might break an index-based operation or a control threshold. A typical subtle bug happens when a value intended for interpolation is stored as an int and later used in fractional math, suddenly losing precision. Another scenario is assuming a non-existent attribute will auto-convert when read; missing attributes typically cause errors or undefined behavior. To reduce surprises, inspect the Geometry Spreadsheet after operations and prefer explicit conversions when the numeric semantics matter. Use naming conventions like global_scale_int to make intent readable. Implicit conversions are not wrong — they are levers. Treat them deliberately and document their use in comments so future you understands the intent.

keyIdea.title: Implicit conversion rule
keyIdea.text: Implicit conversion is convenient but can silently change values; always verify behavior when precision or indexing matters.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Implicit conversions
Comparison
Implicit broadcast vs truncation
See how VEX treats scalar-to-vector and scalar-to-int assignments differently.
Float → Vector (Broadcast)
Assigning 0.5 to @Cd yields {0.5,0.5,0.5}. Useful for uniform color or scale values.
Float → Int (Truncation)
Assigning 5.7 to an int becomes 5. This discards precision and can break index logic.
Practical checklist
  • Inspect the spreadsheet after conversions.
  • Prefer explicit casts when precision or indexing matters.
  • Name attributes to indicate their intended type and purpose.
Misconception

Implicit conversions will always preserve intent. Not true — they may silently alter values and should be used with awareness.

Concrete example
Broadcasting
@Cd = 0.2; // becomes {0.2, 0.2, 0.2}
Truncation
int x = 7.9; // x becomes 7
Key Takeaway

Use implicit conversions when helpful, but verify effects and prefer explicit casts for precise behavior.

screens.title: Explicit conversions and casting patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Explicit conversions, or casting, give you control over how values change type. You can cast with syntax like (int)myFloatValue to force truncation or apply round before casting to preserve intent. For converting floats to vectors, you have two common patterns: construct a vector literal with repeated components or use set() helpers. For example, vector myVec = {myFloat, myFloat, myFloat}; creates a three-component vector from a scalar; alternatively, using set(myFloat, myFloat, myFloat) achieves the same. When you want controlled rounding, call round on the float before casting: int idx = (int)round(myFloat);. Casting is essential when converting primitive data to index usage, or when converting measurement results into discrete buckets. Also remember that casting strings is different; converting numbers to strings uses functions like itoa or sprintf patterns, and string attributes should be handled with care when used as identifiers. A common explicit-write pattern is to read a primitive float, cast it to int, and assign it to a point attribute explicitly: i@prim_id_int = (int)prim_float_val; This leaves no doubt about intent and makes your code resilient during later edits. Casts also document intent for collaborators inspecting the code.

keyIdea.title: Casting practice
keyIdea.text: Use explicit casts and rounding when converting continuous values to discrete ones, and build vectors deliberately from scalar components.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Explicit conversions
Process
Casting steps for safe conversions
  1. Decide target type and intent: discrete index or continuous measure.
  2. If converting to int, choose rounding behavior: truncation vs round() vs floor()/ceil().
  3. Construct vectors explicitly when you need multi-component values rather than relying on implicit broadcasts.
  4. Document casts with comments and type-hinted attribute names.
Pro tip

Use round() before casting when you want conventional rounding instead of truncation.

Code examples
// Cast float to int with rounding
float myFloat = 3.8;
int myInt = (int)round(myFloat); // becomes 4

// Build a uniform color from a float
float val = 0.2;
vector col = {val, val, val};
@Cd = col;

// Explicitly cast primitive read to point int
float prim_float_val = prim(0, "prim_id_float", @primnum);
i@prim_id_int = (int)prim_float_val;
Key Takeaway

Explicit casting makes your intent and numeric behavior explicit; prefer it for conversions that affect logic or indexing.

screens.title: Attribute scope and class
screens.narratorSegment: Attribute scope and class determine where attributes live and how you should read or write them. Point attributes belong to points and typically store position or point-local data. Primitive attributes live on whole primitives such as faces and are used for material assignments or per-primitive properties. Vertex attributes are per-corner values allowing different data for shared vertices, like UV seams. Detail attributes are unique global values that apply across the entire geometry, such as a global scale or seed. When running a wrangle over points, you can access point attributes directly with @ symbols, but to read a primitive attribute you need prim() or to read a detail attribute you use detail(). For example, prim(0, "material_name", @primnum) reads a string material name from the primitive index associated with the current point. Mistakes happen when you assume an attribute exists in the current class. If you try v@myValue when myValue is a float detail attribute, you'll get an error or incorrect behavior. Always inspect the Geometry Spreadsheet to confirm attribute class and type before accessing it. Naming conventions such as suffixing with _pt, _prim, _dt help document class intent and minimize lookup errors.

keyIdea.title: Attribute class rule
keyIdea.text: Attribute class determines storage and access patterns; use functions like prim, point and detail to bridge classes safely.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Attribute scope
Definition
Point, Primitive, Vertex, Detail
Each class controls how data is stored and accessed and affects which functions you must use.
Point
Per-point data such as @P and per-point colors.
Primitive
Per-primitive data like material assignments.
Vertex
Per-corner values, useful for differing UVs on shared points.
Detail
Single global values that affect the whole geometry.
Key Takeaway

Always confirm attribute class when reading or writing. Use prim, point and detail to bridge classes safely.

Practical example
Reading a primitive string from point context
s@prim_material = prim(0, "material_name", @primnum);
Here prim() takes input index, attribute name and primitive index, returning the primitive's value.
Common pitfall

Using the wrong attribute class for a lookup causes errors. Confirm with the Geometry Spreadsheet before accessing.

screens.title: Reading attributes across classes: prim(), point(), detail()
screens.narratorSegment: In practice you'll often need to read an attribute that exists on a different class than the one you're running over. The prim, point and detail functions are your tools for those reads. prim(input, name, primnum) reads a primitive attribute by index; point(input, name, ptnum) reads a point attribute by index; detail(input, name) reads a global value. A concrete scenario: you create a primitive float prim_id_float storing a primitive's number, then run a wrangle over points and use prim to fetch that primitive float for each point. After reading, you might cast it to an int and assign it to a point attribute with an explicit cast. Below is a sample wrangle that reads a primitive attribute, reads a detail integer, and modifies point position based on their combination. Walk calmly through the code and then inspect the Geometry Spreadsheet to confirm attribute types. A common misconception is to expect these functions to implicitly change classes when you forget the correct index; they do not. You must supply the correct component index for reliable results and test with the spreadsheet to validate your read and type assumptions.

keyIdea.title: Read across classes
keyIdea.text: Use prim, point and detail with correct indexes to fetch attributes from other classes, then cast as needed before assignment.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › prim(), point(), detail()
Code walkthrough
// Run Over: Points
// Read a primitive float and a detail integer
float prim_float_val = prim(0, "prim_id_float", @primnum);
i@prim_id_int = (int)prim_float_val; // explicit cast

int detail_scale = detail(0, "global_scale_int");

// Modify point position using the read values
@P.y += (float)i@prim_id_int * detail_scale * 0.1;

// Demonstrate implicit broadcast: float to color
@Cd = prim_float_val / 10.0; // becomes {v,v,v}
Step explanation
Read primitive and detail, cast primitive float to int for index-like use, then update point position and color.
Validation
Open Geometry Spreadsheet to verify prim_id_float, prim_id_int, global_scale_int and the modified @P and @Cd.
Misconception check
prim() won’t implicitly pick the primitive for you unless you supply the correct prim index; confirm with @primnum or computed mapping.
Key Takeaway

When reading across classes, always supply correct indexes and cast results explicitly when they feed logic or indexing operations.

screens.title: Writing attributes across classes with set*attrib functions
screens.narratorSegment: Direct attribute assignment using @ syntax is concise and efficient when you write to the class you're iterating over. However, when you need to create or modify attributes on other components from within a wrangle, the set*attrib family provides explicit, index-based writes. Use setpointattrib(input, name, index, value, mode) to write a value to a specific point by index; setprimattrib and setvertexattrib behave similarly for their classes. setdetailattrib writes a single global value. These functions accept a creation mode such as "set" to create the attribute if it doesn't exist. They are powerful for cross-class updates, but they are also more expensive than direct writes when misused. Prefer them when you are running over one class but must change another, for example writing point colors while iterating primitives. A typical pattern: compute a per-primitive property in a primitive wrangle and then loop over the primitive's points, calling setpointattrib to assign a color per point. Always test in the Geometry Spreadsheet to ensure the attribute exists on the target class and has the expected type. Remember to pay attention to the last argument mode so you don't accidentally append or accumulate values in unintended ways.

keyIdea.title: Use set*attrib sparingly
keyIdea.text: Use set*attrib for explicit cross-class writes but prefer direct @ assignments when writing to the running class for performance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › set*attrib
Architecture
Explicit cross-class writes
Index-based APIs let you write attributes precisely but require correct indexes and modes.
setpointattrib
setpointattrib(0, "Cd", ptIndex, {1,0,0}, "set"); writes color to a given point index.
setprimattrib / setvertexattrib
Same pattern: choose the right target class and supply appropriate index and mode.
setdetailattrib
Write a single global value; useful for configuration-like attributes.
Performance note

These functions are fine when necessary, but prefer direct assignments when writing to the running class to keep nodes efficient.

Example usage
// Inside a Primitive wrangle: write point colors for points of this primitive
int pts[] = primpoints(0, @primnum);
foreach (int pt; pts) {
  setpointattrib(0, "Cd", pt, {1,0,0}, "set");
}

// Create a detail integer
setdetailattrib(0, "global_scale_int", 2, "set");
Key Takeaway

Use set*attrib for targeted writes across classes but be mindful of cost and always validate created attribute names and types in the spreadsheet.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and defensive patterns
screens.narratorSegment: This slide focuses on defensive habits that prevent common mistakes when working with types and attribute functions. First, use clear attribute names that hint at type and class, such as prim_id_float or global_scale_int. These names help you and collaborators quickly locate attributes in the Geometry Spreadsheet. Second, verify attributes visually after you run a wrangle: check the target class column in the spreadsheet to confirm the attribute type and class. Third, prefer explicit casts when converting data used for indexing or control decisions; this prevents silent truncation from changing program logic. Fourth, when reading from another class, validate that the index you pass is correct. For example, reading a primitive attribute from a point scope requires @primnum or a mapping function to compute the correct prim index. Fifth, prefer building vectors explicitly from scalars when the shape matters to downstream code, rather than relying on broadcasted values that might go unnoticed. Regularly use small test wrangles and spreadsheet inspection as a rapid unit test for your attribute logic — it catches problems before they ripple through a larger network. Common pitfalls and defensive patterns means name attributes clearly, validate types in the spreadsheet, cast explicitly for index-like values, and confirm indexes when reading across classes.. In practical terms, how to avoid errors: naming, spreadsheet checks, and explicit casts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Guided lab: reproduce the Attribute Wrangle
Follow these steps and validate in the Geometry Spreadsheet.
Step 1 — Geometry setup
Create Grid SOP and two Attribute Create SOPs: prim_id_float (Primitive, Float, $PR) and global_scale_int (Detail, Integer, 2).
Step 2 — Wrangle code
Add Attribute Wrangle running over Points and paste the provided code to read prim and detail values, cast, and modify @P and @Cd.
// Run Over: Points
float prim_float_val = prim(0, "prim_id_float", @primnum);
i@prim_id_int = (int)prim_float_val;
int detail_scale = detail(0, "global_scale_int");
@P.y += (float)i@prim_id_int * detail_scale * 0.1;
@Cd = prim_float_val / 10.0;

Open Geometry Spreadsheet and check Point, Primitive, and Detail tabs for the new attributes and their types.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll build a clear mental model of how VEX represents data and how Houdini moves values between types and attribute classes. We'll review the basic VEX types — integer, float, vectors of two, three and four components, and strings — and then focus on how conversions happen, both implicitly and when you explicitly cast. You will see practical examples of where implicit casting helps and where it silently causes data loss, and we'll establish safe patterns you can use right away. We'll also cover attribute scope: point, primitive, vertex and detail, and how functions like prim, point, and detail enable reading across those scopes. Finally, we'll walk through controlled attribute writes using setpointattrib and related functions, so you can create or modify attributes on other components without surprises. By the end you will be able to choose the correct type, avoid common mismatches, and explain why explicit casts sometimes prevent subtle bugs. Consider a simple float driving color: small choices here change whether color becomes a uniform grey or an intended RGB value. Keep that contrast in mind as you explore the examples.

These four objectives frame practical skills you can apply immediately when authoring VEX. First, you will accurately identify and use VEX native types: integers, floats, vector2, vector, vector4 and strings. This means you will choose the correct storage type for positions, UVs, colors, and identifiers to avoid downstream errors. Second, you'll explain and demonstrate both implicit and explicit conversions. You will show examples that reveal safe broadcasting and places where implicit truncation hides precision loss. Third, you'll understand attribute scope and class — point, primitive, vertex and detail — and how attribute class affects where data lives and how functions access it. You will practice reading a primitive attribute while running over points and vice versa. Fourth, you'll use the explicit set*attrib functions safely: setpointattrib, setprimattrib, setvertexattrib and setdetailattrib, knowing when these are necessary and what their cost is compared to direct assignments. Each objective ties a conceptual idea to an actionable outcome so you can verify competency in the Geometry Spreadsheet and in a wrangle node.

This second objectives slide defines assessable outcomes and practical checks you can perform. You will run small wrangles that intentionally convert types and inspect results in the Geometry Spreadsheet. For example, you will cast a float to an int and confirm truncation, then use round before casting to preserve intent. You will broadcast a float into a vector for a uniform color and then convert it back to a scalar when needed. You will also read a primitive float while running over points using prim and convert it to an integer attribute on points with an explicit cast. Finally, you will write attributes across classes using setpointattrib and then open the spreadsheet to verify the attribute's class and type. These steps create reproducible checks: the code, the spreadsheet, and visual geometry changes together prove competency. By practicing these patterns you reduce silent bugs and better reason about data provenance in complex Houdini networks.

Let's define the primary VEX types and place them into practical contexts you’ll use every day. An int is a whole number used for counts, indices, or discrete flags. A float stores real numbers with fractional precision and is the workhorse for measurements and continuous values. Vector2 stores two floats, useful for UV coordinates; vector stores three floats and is the canonical type for positions, normals and 3D directions; vector4 packs four floats and commonly represents color with alpha. String is used for text, like material names or identifiers. Each type has semantic meaning: choose int for loop counters and array indexes, float for scale factors and weights, vector for spatial data and color triples, and string for names. A common mistake is using a vector where a float was intended, which complicates math operations and causes type errors. Another pitfall is storing an index as a float – it may work in some contexts but can create subtle bugs when compared or used as an index. To ground this, consider @P as a vector holding vertex positions, @uv as a vector2 for texture coordinates, and @Cd as a vector for color. When you pick types with intention, your wrangles become clearer and less error-prone. Try to name attributes in a way that hints at their type, such as prim_id_float or global_scale_int, so the spreadsheet tells the story.

Implicit conversions are a convenience built into VEX, but they carry trade-offs you must understand. When you assign a float to an int, VEX truncates the fractional part. When you assign a float to a vector, the float broadcasts to every component producing a uniform vector. These behaviors are handy: you can set a uniform color or a uniform offset with a single scalar. But implicit truncation can hide logic errors. For example, assigning 5.7 to an int yields 5, which might break an index-based operation or a control threshold. A typical subtle bug happens when a value intended for interpolation is stored as an int and later used in fractional math, suddenly losing precision. Another scenario is assuming a non-existent attribute will auto-convert when read; missing attributes typically cause errors or undefined behavior. To reduce surprises, inspect the Geometry Spreadsheet after operations and prefer explicit conversions when the numeric semantics matter. Use naming conventions like global_scale_int to make intent readable. Implicit conversions are not wrong — they are levers. Treat them deliberately and document their use in comments so future you understands the intent.

Explicit conversions, or casting, give you control over how values change type. You can cast with syntax like (int)myFloatValue to force truncation or apply round before casting to preserve intent. For converting floats to vectors, you have two common patterns: construct a vector literal with repeated components or use set() helpers. For example, vector myVec = {myFloat, myFloat, myFloat}; creates a three-component vector from a scalar; alternatively, using set(myFloat, myFloat, myFloat) achieves the same. When you want controlled rounding, call round on the float before casting: int idx = (int)round(myFloat);. Casting is essential when converting primitive data to index usage, or when converting measurement results into discrete buckets. Also remember that casting strings is different; converting numbers to strings uses functions like itoa or sprintf patterns, and string attributes should be handled with care when used as identifiers. A common explicit-write pattern is to read a primitive float, cast it to int, and assign it to a point attribute explicitly: i@prim_id_int = (int)prim_float_val; This leaves no doubt about intent and makes your code resilient during later edits. Casts also document intent for collaborators inspecting the code.

Attribute scope and class determine where attributes live and how you should read or write them. Point attributes belong to points and typically store position or point-local data. Primitive attributes live on whole primitives such as faces and are used for material assignments or per-primitive properties. Vertex attributes are per-corner values allowing different data for shared vertices, like UV seams. Detail attributes are unique global values that apply across the entire geometry, such as a global scale or seed. When running a wrangle over points, you can access point attributes directly with @ symbols, but to read a primitive attribute you need prim() or to read a detail attribute you use detail(). For example, prim(0, "material_name", @primnum) reads a string material name from the primitive index associated with the current point. Mistakes happen when you assume an attribute exists in the current class. If you try v@myValue when myValue is a float detail attribute, you'll get an error or incorrect behavior. Always inspect the Geometry Spreadsheet to confirm attribute class and type before accessing it. Naming conventions such as suffixing with _pt, _prim, _dt help document class intent and minimize lookup errors.

In practice you'll often need to read an attribute that exists on a different class than the one you're running over. The prim, point and detail functions are your tools for those reads. prim(input, name, primnum) reads a primitive attribute by index; point(input, name, ptnum) reads a point attribute by index; detail(input, name) reads a global value. A concrete scenario: you create a primitive float prim_id_float storing a primitive's number, then run a wrangle over points and use prim to fetch that primitive float for each point. After reading, you might cast it to an int and assign it to a point attribute with an explicit cast. Below is a sample wrangle that reads a primitive attribute, reads a detail integer, and modifies point position based on their combination. Walk calmly through the code and then inspect the Geometry Spreadsheet to confirm attribute types. A common misconception is to expect these functions to implicitly change classes when you forget the correct index; they do not. You must supply the correct component index for reliable results and test with the spreadsheet to validate your read and type assumptions.

Direct attribute assignment using @ syntax is concise and efficient when you write to the class you're iterating over. However, when you need to create or modify attributes on other components from within a wrangle, the set*attrib family provides explicit, index-based writes. Use setpointattrib(input, name, index, value, mode) to write a value to a specific point by index; setprimattrib and setvertexattrib behave similarly for their classes. setdetailattrib writes a single global value. These functions accept a creation mode such as "set" to create the attribute if it doesn't exist. They are powerful for cross-class updates, but they are also more expensive than direct writes when misused. Prefer them when you are running over one class but must change another, for example writing point colors while iterating primitives. A typical pattern: compute a per-primitive property in a primitive wrangle and then loop over the primitive's points, calling setpointattrib to assign a color per point. Always test in the Geometry Spreadsheet to ensure the attribute exists on the target class and has the expected type. Remember to pay attention to the last argument mode so you don't accidentally append or accumulate values in unintended ways.
